messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At seven, Malik’s world contracted to the space between his bedroom door and the hallway floor. The physical abuse by his caregiver was a recurring storm, marked by sudden escalations that left no warning. What frightened him most was the sheer unpredictability of it; he learned to brace for the moment the quiet would shatter. Over time, his mind shielded him by locking the door to the past. When he tried deliberately to remember those nights, he found himself staring at a blank wall in his own head, unable to pull the events into focus. Yet when the memories slipped out, they came in disconnected pieces: the sharp crack of a belt buckle, the smell of spilled liquor, the heavy thud of boots on linoleum. These fragments did not fit together, but they arrived with a visceral clarity that made them feel more real than ordinary days. He would sit long after the sun went down, certain the past was breathing down his neck, though he could not name what was coming. As years passed, the ghost of those nights dictated his routines. He kept every photograph carefully tucked away, convinced that opening an album would release something he could no longer contain. When a college roommate once joked about digitizing old pictures, Malik’s stomach dropped; he quickly claimed he had lost the album, his voice tight with a fear he could not explain. He began to steer clear of sudden changes. A last-minute meeting or a friend showing up unannounced sent his pulse hammering, his body automatically bracing for an impact that never came. More often, he found himself exhausted each morning, waking from nightmares with his sheets tangled around his legs and a lingering sense of dread. He would lie there, counting his breaths until the residue of the dream faded, telling himself he was fine, though his hands trembled. Now, at twenty-two, Malik served as principal of a charter school, a role demanding steady hands and unwavering presence. His office became a landscape of careful navigation. When the district administrator called unexpectedly to shift his weekly agenda, Malik felt his chest tighten, his mind racing with the same helpless dread he had known as a child. He had come to believe he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that chaos would always slip through the cracks he tried to patch. The administrative demands forced him into rigid routines: arriving early, scripting his day hour by hour, avoiding open common areas where surprises could materialize. His girlfriend, Amara, noticed how he withdrew when plans shifted, how he sat perfectly still during conversations, as if listening for a threat only he could hear. He was certain he had permanently changed for the worse, that the boy who took the beatings had simply moved into his adult bones. What frightened him most was the quiet suspicion that his anger was a live wire. He imagined losing control and doing something terrible, so he began to distance himself preemptively, fearing his own temper more than any external danger. By his senior year, the weight became impossible to carry alone. The fragmented memories surfaced during staff meetings, sharp and uninvited, while his fear of rage kept him from raising his voice even when students defied him. He stopped going to group dinners, avoided old yearbooks, and learned to leave his bedroom door cracked open each night. It was a cracked spine that finally brought him to the counseling center. The administrator had handed him a referral form, but Malik signed it himself, his handwriting steady despite the fear pooling in his stomach. He did not know if talking to someone could mend his fractured past or quiet the certainty that he was fundamentally broken. He only knew he could no longer outrun the silence, and he hoped, desperately, that there was a way to stop waiting for the next blow.
